one_child_she_version.text: Last time: a cold, wet fox tapped at the last lit window in Candlemere, with news that the beacon on Wardlow had gone out.
In the morning, Candlemere was grey. No chimney smoked, not one lamp flickered, and every window on the lane looked as sleepy as a yawn. Somebody had to carry Grandma's flame to Wardlow, and soon.
"Let's ask the neighbors," said Tamsin. "A grown-up will go."
Grandma stood in the doorway, where she could see the whole lane. "Every door," she said. "And stay where I can see you."
So off went Tamsin down the lane, with Ember trotting close beside, her magnificent tail held high out of the puddles.
The baker opened the bakehouse door in a puff of flour. "Someone should," he said. "But not I. The bread won't bake itself."
"Good morning," said Ember, very politely.
But all the baker heard was *yip, yip*. "Noisy fox," he said, not unkindly, and shut the door.
Ember sniffed. Nobody had ever called her noisy before.
Next door, the miller came out slowly, rubbing his knees. "Not I," he said. "These old knees won't climb Wardlow."
Then Reeve Osric hurried past with his arms full of tally-sticks. "Yes, yes," he said. "We'll see to it tomorrow."
At one window a face peeped out. "Too far, in the dark," it whispered, and the curtain dropped.
"How many dark windows will there be by tomorrow?" whispered Tamsin.
"One, two, three, four, lots," whispered Ember.
Everybody agreed that someone should go. But nobody was willing to be the one. At every door the answer was the same: "Not I."
Then Will, the baker's boy, came pelting round the corner. "I'll go right now," he shouted, "and I dare anybody to stop me!" Off he ran into the old holloway, with no light at all.
The holloway, a sunken track under the trees, was dark even at noon, though its mouth was in sight of Grandma's doorway.
Tamsin wanted to take the dare too, and run in after him. But part of her wanted to run home and hide under the quilt. Tamsin didn't move, and neither did Ember.
*Splosh!* Before anyone could count to twenty, Will was back, muddy from top to toe, a little sheepish, and looking hard at his boots.
"There's a puddle," said Will, "in the dark."
Nobody laughed. Ember went and stood right next to the muddy boy, so Will wouldn't be muddy all on his own. Tamsin wiped the worst of the mud off with a sleeve.

By the Moot Hall door, in plain sight of Grandma's doorway, sat old Hild the wick-woman with her tray of wicks. Grandma had bought wicks from her for years. Hild's donkey, Dun, dozed at her side. On the door behind her hung an old notice.
Tamsin read it out loud: "Beacon Night. All welcome. Bring one stick, and a friend."
Old Brock lay on the step, and did not get up for anyone. Tamsin stopped to pat him anyway.
"Good morning," said Ember.
"Good morning, fox," said Hild, as if foxes said good morning to her every day.
Tamsin stared. The wick-woman could understand Ember too!
Then Hild beckoned Tamsin close, while Ember tried to count the wicks and got as far as lots.
Hild looked at Tamsin for a long, quiet moment. "How big must a person be to carry a lantern?" asked Hild.
Tamsin opened her mouth, and shut it again. Hild only waited, the way old folk wait for a kettle to sing.
Then Hild gave Tamsin something from the tray that wasn't on it at all: a question, to keep in a pocket. "For when I'm not there," said Hild. "There will be more, one day."
To Tamsin: "What's the brave thing, and what's the silly thing?"
Last of all, Hild put a little brass bell into Tamsin's hand. "Ring it if you ever lose your way," said Hild. "Stand still, ring, and call."
Tamsin looked at the bell, and then at Will, muddy and bedraggled on the step. Then out went the bell, and a hand too. "You carry the bell."
Will took the bell, and the hand. *Ting-a-ling!* Not one bit sheepish now, Will rang it all the way back up the lane, loud and proud. Here and there a curtain twitched.
Ember trotted beside him with her ears folded flat, looking pained.
At the cottage gate, Will gave the bell back with a grin. "On Beacon Night," he said, "I'll carry a stick up Wardlow myself."
"Stand still, ring, and call," said Tamsin, and put the bell safe in a pocket.
Back by the fire, Grandma listened to all of it.

Tamsin looked into the fire, thinking about the long road and the dark, and her tummy went wobbly. Nobody on the whole lane had been willing. Then Tamsin stood up, held an invisible lantern up high, and took one step forward.
"I'll help," she said. "With a proper light, and all of us together. Lantern up!"
A hush fell over the cottage. Then the fire gave a small pop, as if it agreed.
Tamsin packed the little backpack. In went the apples, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven.
"One, two, three, four, lots," said Ember helpfully.
"Seven!" said Tamsin.
"And I shall come too," said Ember. "Somebody has to know the way, and foxes are extremely good at roads."
Tamsin pulled on her boots. Ember tried to help, and got a fox's nose stuck in one.
Grandma laughed, and pulled the boot off Ember's nose. "Nobody's too small to carry a light," she said. "But nobody carries it alone."

That night the brass bell sat on the mantel by the note from home. Ember slept curled on the quilt like a warm red scarf, and the apples slept in the backpack. Tamsin fell asleep last, with Hild's question still there, like a smooth stone in a pocket.

flags_for_jon: one_child_she_version is rendered by render-chapter.py's own code for a one-child 'she' family (eldest band 7-9, grandparent 'Grandma', two parents), named with the checker's placeholder (now "Tamsin").
The signs and talker versions of the youngest's "Who needs help?" and "You carry the bell" keep the same act and result.
Picture blocks (pic2.*) carry the grandparent, the bell, the pocket questions, the youngest's act, the apples and boots, the grandparent's "Nobody's too small…" and the ending for every family size.

New in the checker pass: ch2.door.gp and ch2.hild.gp (Hild known to the grandparent, and everything in sight of the doorway), ch2.bellback (the bell's rule said back at the gate), ch2.p35.one (the one-child boots, with a "she" version that names the fox's nose).

New in the revision pass: pic2.pull (picture 3's two pulls in one sentence, so the sample family has two four-sentence pictures, not three) and pic2.bellback (the bell's rule said back at the gate in picture 9). pic2.end's one-child version now matches the master (Ember on the quilt).
